quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A room where students learn lessons together.
A building or room with many books to read or borrow.
A room where people go to do work, often at a desk.

quests.hint: Each of these is a place, but people go there for different reasons.
quests.explanation: A classroom is where lessons happen, while a library is a quieter place built around books. An office breaks the pattern — people go there to work, not to study or read.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: To remove dirt from something using water.
To remove water or wetness from something.
To remove dirt or mess to make something tidy.

quests.hint: These three actions often happen one after another, like doing laundry.
quests.explanation: You wash something to remove dirt with water, then dry it to remove the water itself. Clean is the broader word — it covers the whole job of making something tidy, not just one step.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A married man, in relation to his spouse.
A married woman, in relation to her spouse.
A young person, or someone's son or daughter.

quests.hint: These words describe people connected by marriage and family.
quests.explanation: Husband and wife describe two married partners — one male, one female. Child is a different kind of family word; it describes a son or daughter, not a spouse.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: A tool with a small bowl shape, used for eating soup or soft food.
A tool with pointed prongs, used for picking up food.
A tool with a sharp edge, used for cutting food.

quests.hint: You'll find all three of these next to your plate at dinner.
quests.explanation: A spoon works well for soup or anything soft, while a fork is better for holding solid pieces of food still. A knife takes on a different job entirely — cutting the food into smaller pieces.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: To raise something up from a lower position.
To move something toward yourself using force.
To hold and move something from one place to another.

quests.hint: Each of these actions describes what your arms can do with a heavy object.
quests.explanation: Lift means raising something up, while pull means dragging it toward you. Carry is different from both — it's about moving something from place to place once you're already holding it.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: At every time, without exception.
At no time, not ever.
On some occasions, but not every time.

quests.hint: These words tell you how often something happens, from all the time to none at all.
quests.explanation: Always and never sit at opposite ends of frequency — one means every time, the other means not once. Sometimes lands in the middle, describing something that happens on occasion but not consistently.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A folding tool you hold above you to stay dry in the rain.
A piece of clothing worn over other clothes to keep warm.
Sturdy shoes that cover the foot and ankle, often worn in bad weather.

quests.hint: You might reach for all three of these on a cold, rainy day.
quests.explanation: An umbrella keeps rain off your head, while a coat keeps your body warm. Boots handle a different part of the job — protecting your feet from cold or wet ground.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: To take something with a plan to give it back later.
To let someone use something of yours, expecting it back.
To give something back to its owner.

quests.hint: Two of these describe opposite sides of the same exchange.
quests.explanation: Borrow and lend describe the same event from two different people's viewpoints — one takes, the other gives. Return closes the story: it's the final step, when the item goes back to its owner.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A hard, white part inside your mouth used for chewing.
One of the five thin parts at the end of your hand.
The part of your body used for hearing.

quests.hint: Each word names a small but important part of the body.
quests.explanation: A tooth helps you chew, a finger helps you hold and touch things, and an ear lets you hear sounds. Each one has a clearly different job on the body.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: Having clear skies with bright sunshine.
Having the sky covered mostly by clouds.
Having strong-moving air.

quests.hint: Look up — is the sky clear, covered, or is the air simply moving fast?
quests.explanation: Sunny and cloudy both describe how the sky looks, but in opposite ways — one is bright, the other is covered. Windy describes something else altogether: how strongly the air is moving, not how the sky looks.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: Having a taste like sugar.
Having a sharp, acidic taste like a lemon.
Having a taste like salt.

quests.hint: Imagine tasting sugar, then a lemon, then a potato chip.
quests.explanation: Sweet reminds most people of sugar, while sour brings a sharp taste like biting into a lemon. Salty takes yet another direction, matching the taste of salt itself.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: A road in a town or city, usually with buildings on each side.
An open, green area for relaxing or playing outdoors.
A structure built to cross over a river, road, or valley.

quests.hint: Each word names something you'd pass while walking through a city.
quests.explanation: A street is lined with buildings and traffic, while a park is an open green space for relaxing. A bridge serves a very different purpose — it simply helps you cross from one side to another.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A small case used to carry money and cards.
Small metal tools used to lock or unlock something.
Lenses worn over the eyes to help you see better.

quests.hint: These are three small items people often check for before leaving the house.
quests.explanation: A wallet holds your money and cards, while keys let you lock and unlock doors. Glasses handle a completely different job — helping your eyes see clearly.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: To reach a place after traveling.
To go away from a place.
To remain in a place without leaving.

quests.hint: Picture a trip: one word starts it, one word ends it, and one word pauses it.
quests.explanation: Arrive marks the moment you reach a place, while leave marks the moment you go. Stay works differently from both — it means staying put, without any movement at all.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: Able to be done without much effort.
Hard to do, needing real effort.
Not able to be done at all.

quests.hint: Rank these from something simple to something that truly cannot be done.
quests.explanation: Easy and difficult sit at two points on the same scale, describing how much effort a task takes. Impossible goes past both of them — it means the task can't be done no matter how much effort you give it.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: A soft cushion you rest your head on while sleeping.
A large piece of soft fabric used to keep warm in bed.
A piece of glass that shows your reflection.

quests.hint: Two of these are for sleeping, and one is for checking how you look.
quests.explanation: A pillow supports your head, and a blanket keeps your whole body warm — both are made for sleeping. A mirror has nothing to do with sleep at all; it simply reflects whatever stands in front of it.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: To put a question to someone.
To reply to a question.
To describe something clearly so it can be understood.

quests.hint: These words describe the back-and-forth of a conversation.
quests.explanation: Ask starts the exchange with a question, and answer responds to it directly. Explain goes further than a simple answer — it means giving enough detail for something to be truly understood.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: Having nothing inside.
Holding as much as possible; not able to hold more.
Damaged and no longer working correctly.

quests.hint: Two of these describe how much is inside something — the third describes its condition.
quests.explanation: Empty and full are opposites that describe how much is inside a container. Broken changes the subject entirely — it's about damage and condition, not about how much space is used.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A small piece of paper or digital pass that lets you travel or enter somewhere.
An official document that proves your identity when traveling abroad.
A case used to carry clothes and belongings while traveling.

quests.hint: You'd need to check for all three of these before a flight abroad.
quests.explanation: A ticket lets you board, and a passport proves who you are once you land. A suitcase serves a different purpose altogether — it simply carries your belongings along with you.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: To prepare food using heat, in any way.
To cook food using dry heat, usually in an oven.
To cook food in water that has reached its highest temperature.

quests.hint: One of these is a general word, and the other two describe specific methods.
quests.explanation: Cook is the general word for preparing food with heat, no matter the method. Bake and boil are two specific ways of doing that — one uses an oven, and the other uses bubbling water.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A boy or man with the same parents as you.
The child of your aunt or uncle.
The mother of your mother or father.

quests.hint: Each word describes a family member from a different branch of the family tree.
quests.explanation: A brother shares your own parents, while a cousin comes from your aunt or uncle's side of the family. A grandmother sits in a different generation entirely — she's a parent of one of your own parents.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: A message sent electronically over the internet.
A secret word or code used to protect an account.
A wireless connection that lets devices access the internet.

quests.hint: All three of these are things you need to check your messages online.
quests.explanation: An email is the message itself, while a password is what protects your account from other people. Wifi plays a different role — it's the connection that lets your device reach the internet in the first place.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: In good physical condition, without illness.
Feeling unwell or suffering from an illness.
To relax or sleep in order to recover energy.

quests.hint: Two of these describe how your body feels, and one describes what helps it.
quests.explanation: Healthy and sick sit at opposite ends of wellbeing — one means you're well, the other means you're not. Rest is different from both; it's an action you take, often to move from sick back toward healthy.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: A story shown on screen through moving pictures.
A piece of music with words, meant to be sung.
An activity played for fun, often with rules.

quests.hint: Each word names a different way people enjoy their free time.
quests.explanation: A movie tells a story through pictures, and a song delivers a message through music. A game takes a different form again — it invites you to actively play, not just watch or listen.

quests.instruction: Match each expression with its meaning.

pairs.value: Words used to politely get someone's attention or apologize for a small interruption.
Words used to show gratitude for something.
A word added to a request to make it more polite.

quests.hint: All three of these are polite phrases you'll use many times a day.
quests.explanation: Excuse me helps you politely interrupt or get attention, while thank you shows gratitude after someone helps you. Please works earlier in that timeline — it softens a request before anyone has done anything yet.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A printed or digital record showing what you paid for.
A reduction in the usual price of something.
A person who takes payments at a shop or store.

quests.hint: Each word relates to a different moment in the process of paying at a store.
quests.explanation: A discount lowers the price before you pay, and a cashier is the person who takes your payment. A receipt comes last of all — it's your proof of the purchase after everything is done.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.value: Close to something in distance.
A long distance away from something.
In the space that separates two things.

quests.hint: These words describe where one thing is compared to another.
quests.explanation: Near and far are opposites that describe distance — one is close, the other isn't. Between describes something else entirely: a position in the middle, with something on each side.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: Flames that burn and produce heat and light.
The gray or black cloud that rises from something burning.
A way out of a building, especially in an emergency.

quests.hint: If one of these appears, you should look for the other right away.
quests.explanation: Fire is the flame itself, and smoke is the cloud it produces as it burns. An exit is your safe response to both — the way out if either one puts you in danger.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: To keep information in your mind and recall it later.
To fail to remember something.
To gain new knowledge or a new skill.

quests.hint: One of these happens before the other two even become possible.
quests.explanation: You have to learn something before you can either remember or forget it. Remember and forget are opposites that come afterward, describing whether that information stays in your mind or slips away.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: Free from harm or risk.
Likely to cause harm or injury.
Paying close attention to avoid mistakes or harm.

quests.hint: Two of these describe a situation, and one describes how a person behaves in it.
quests.explanation: Safe and dangerous describe a place or situation — one carries little risk, the other carries a lot. Careful describes a person's behavior instead, especially the kind of behavior that helps turn a dangerous situation into a safe one.
